intro: Nobody has dated a single one of Fort Worth's big trees, and that turns out to be the interesting part. What the city has instead are measurements: a Texas Red Oak 622 centimetres round on a strip of grass beside a residential parkway, a national champion mesquite of a species ranchers pay to bulldoze, and the largest jujube on record in Texas. Four verified trees, two walkable pairs, and four open questions we would like a reader to help close.
meta_description: Fort Worth's biggest tree is a Texas Red Oak 622 centimetres round on Ward Parkway. Four verified remarkable trees and how to reach each one.
question_meta: No tree in Fort Worth has a documented age. The biggest is a Texas Red Oak 622 centimetres round on Ward Parkway. Where to find it and three more.
question_answer: Nobody has established the oldest tree in Fort Worth, and we would rather say so than guess. The largest by trunk is the Texas Red Oak on Ward Parkway in the south of the city, 622 centimetres round when the Texas Big Tree Registry taped it in July 2026. If you know of a dated tree here, tell us.
question_context: Fort Worth's remarkable trees are recorded by size rather than by age. The Texas Big Tree Registry measures girth, height and crown spread and certifies champions on a points system, and none of its fields carries a planting date or a ring count. Age can sometimes be derived from girth using a published growth rate, but these four are a Texas Red Oak, a honey mesquite, a Texas ash and a jujube, and the rates for those in north Texas conditions are not settled enough to put a number on the page. So the field stays empty. What is documented is unusually good: the Ward Parkway red oak and the Will Rogers mesquite are both stops on the DFW National Champion Tree Trail, the Pioneers Rest ash has been professionally treated against the emerald ash borer at the city's expense since 2019, and the Botanic Garden's jujube is the state record for its species. Three of the four are free to visit. The trees fall into two walks: the Botanic Garden and the Will Rogers Memorial Center sit about a kilometre apart in the Cultural District, and the Pioneers Rest ash is walkable from Sundance Square downtown.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Fort Worth?
faq.a: Nobody has dated one. The trees here are recorded by size rather than age, and we would rather leave the field empty than invent a number. If you know of a dated tree in Fort Worth, we would like to hear about it.

faq.q: What is the biggest tree in Fort Worth?
faq.a: The Texas Red Oak on Ward Parkway, 622 centimetres round when the Texas Big Tree Registry measured it in July 2026. It stands on city park land beside a residential parkway in the south of the city, near TCU.

faq.q: Are Fort Worth's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Three of the four are. The Ward Parkway red oak, the Will Rogers mesquite and the Pioneers Rest ash all stand on public land at no charge. The jujube is inside the Fort Worth Botanic Garden, which charges general admission of 14 dollars for adults.

Between two of them. The Botanic Garden and the Will Rogers Memorial Center are about a kilometre apart in the Cultural District, roughly 4.5 kilometres west of downtown. The Pioneers Rest ash is a separate walk, about 1.2 kilometres northeast of downtown and reachable on foot from Sundance Square. The Ward Parkway oak is 5 kilometres south with no rail stop nearby.

faq.q: Why does a mesquite count as a remarkable tree?
faq.a: Because of what it took to get that big. Honey mesquite is treated as a pest across Texas rangeland and ranchers spend real money clearing it, so a specimen that reaches 478 centimetres round has outlived a great deal of intent to remove it. It is a national champion for the species.

trees.name: The Jujube of the Botanic Garden

location.address: Near the intersection of Old Garden Road and Rock Springs Road, Fort Worth Botanic Garden, 3220 Botanic Garden Blvd, Fort Worth, TX
location.neighbourhood: Fort Worth Botanic Garden (Rock Springs section), Cultural District

verified_sources: Texas Big Tree Registry (TAMU Forest Service), TreeID 436, lead source only
trees.access: Paid entry. Fort Worth Botanic Garden charges general admission (adults $14, ages 3-15 $8, as of the fee restructure that folded the former separate Japanese Garden charge into one ticket). Open during garden hours.
trees.transport: Inside the Fort Worth Botanic Garden grounds, Cultural District, about 4.5 km west of downtown Fort Worth; no direct rail, nearest Trinity Metro bus routes serve the Cultural District.
trees.story:
The largest jujube on record in Texas is a Chinese fruit tree, and it stands about five metres off a road in Fort Worth. The Botanic Garden's champion runs to roughly 13.7 metres tall, which is a lot of height for a species usually kept as a squat orchard tree with the fruit inside a ladder's reach. Its trunk is 190 centimetres round. The Texas Big Tree Registry took that measurement in May 2020, and the regional tree trail that maps the garden's champions calls it the biggest of its kind recorded in the state.

Jujube has been grown in Chinese orchards for thousands of years and came to America as a crop rather than as an ornament. The fruit ripens green to a wrinkled red brown and eats like a dry apple, sweeter as it shrivels. Most people walking the corner of Old Garden Road and Rock Springs Road go past it without registering that they are looking at a state record, because it does not look like one: no buttressed trunk, no fence, no plaque doing the work for it.

Nobody has dated this tree and no source we can find has tried, so if you know when it went in, tell us. The garden charges 14 dollars for adults, which covers the whole grounds, and the champion trail passes several other record holders on the way round.

trees.name: The Ward Parkway Texas Red Oak

location.address: 2026-2212 Ward Parkway, Fort Worth, TX 76110 (city-owned park land along the parkway)
location.neighbourhood: Park Hill, near TCU and Colonial Country Club

verified_sources: Texas Big Tree Registry (TAMU Forest Service), TreeID 843, lead source only
trees.access: Free. On city-owned park land along Ward Parkway; texastreetrails.org states plainly 'the public can visit the trees within park operating hours.'
trees.transport: In south Fort Worth near TCU, about 5 km south of downtown; no rail stop nearby, reachable by Trinity Metro bus or a short drive/rideshare.
trees.story:
Its trunk is nearly two metres thick, and it grows on a strip of municipal grass beside a residential parkway. The Texas Red Oak on Ward Parkway measures 622 centimetres round, recorded by the Texas Big Tree Registry in July 2026, and the DFW National Champion Tree Trail lists it as stop two on a route of national title holders.

That size is the whole point. Texas red oak is a tree of limestone hills and canyon rims, a well shaped and fairly modest oak that people plant for its autumn colour rather than for bulk, and this one has grown to a girth the species is not supposed to reach. It did it in plain sight, in south Fort Worth between TCU and the Colonial Country Club, with no fence around it, no ticket, no visitor centre and nothing on the ground to tell you what you are standing under. The land is city owned and open in park hours. Traffic goes by four metres away.

Nobody has dated it. There is no ring count, no planting record and no growth figure for the species we would trust enough to work backwards from, so the age stays an open question rather than a number we made up. If you have seen one published, send it to us. The tape measure is the fact that holds, and at 622 centimetres it does not need any help.

trees.name: The Will Rogers Mesquite

location.address: Will Rogers Road South, Will Rogers Memorial Center grounds, Fort Worth, TX 76107
location.neighbourhood: Will Rogers Memorial Center, Cultural District

verified_sources: Texas Big Tree Registry (TAMU Forest Service), TreeID 781, lead source only
https://www.texastreetrails.org/tours/natchamp_trail.html (DFW National Champion Tree Trail, Tree ID 128, National Champion Mesquite)
trees.access: Free. City-owned park land at the Will Rogers Memorial Center; texastreetrails.org states it 'can be visited within park operating hours.'
trees.transport: In the Cultural District, about 4.5 km west of downtown Fort Worth, near the Fort Worth Botanic Garden and museums; reachable by Trinity Metro bus.
trees.story:
Texas ranchers spend real money bulldozing mesquite, and this one is a national champion. The honey mesquite on the Will Rogers Memorial Center grounds measures 478 centimetres round, taped by the Texas Big Tree Registry in June 2024; an ordinary mature mesquite rarely passes 200. The DFW National Champion Tree Trail names it the national champion of its species, and that crown is the trail's claim rather than a permanent title, because the American Forests register turns over and champions get dethroned. The trunk is not in dispute.

Mesquite is the tree Texas treats as a weed. It is thorny, crooked, deep rooted and almost impossible to kill, it takes over grazing land, it gets cleared by the acre, and then it ends up in the smoker giving brisket its flavour. Almost nothing is allowed to grow old. This one did, on city ground beside the halls where the Fort Worth Stock Show fills the complex every winter, watched by crowds who came for the livestock and walked past a record without looking up.

Nobody has recorded its age, and mesquite growth swings so hard with rainfall that a guess would be worth nothing. If you have seen a figure, tell us. It stands free and unfenced in the Cultural District, a short walk from the Botanic Garden.

trees.name: The Pioneers Rest Texas Ash

location.address: Pioneers Rest Cemetery, 620 Samuels Avenue, Fort Worth, TX 76102
location.neighbourhood: Near Sundance Square / downtown Fort Worth

verified_sources: Texas Big Tree Registry (TAMU Forest Service), TreeID 19, lead source only
trees.access: Free. Public historic cemetery (National Register of Historic Places, 2021), 620 Samuels Avenue. The main gate is sometimes locked but a public entrance exists on the south end of the west fence; visiting in daylight is recommended. Maintained by the Pioneers Rest Cemetery Association with city involvement.
trees.transport: About 1.2 km northeast of downtown Fort Worth, near Sundance Square, walkable from the city centre.
trees.story:
Fort Worth pays to keep this one tree alive. In 2019 the city had the Texas Ash in Pioneers Rest Cemetery professionally injected against the emerald ash borer, the beetle that has been erasing ash trees across North America, with a commitment to come back and repeat the treatment every two or three years. That is an unusual amount of attention for a single ash, and it is the regional champion of its species, 213 centimetres round.

It grows in the oldest burial ground in the city, on Samuels Avenue, just over a kilometre northeast of downtown and walkable from it, among Fort Worth's earliest graves. The cemetery went onto the National Register of Historic Places in 2021. The ash stands over the kind of ground where the city's own beginning is written on the stones, and it is being kept going against a pest that has already killed hundreds of millions of its relatives.

Proof of life here is better than most: the Texas Big Tree Registry put a tape around this exact trunk in December 2025. Its age is unrecorded, and there is no growth figure for Texas ash we trust enough to work backwards from, so we leave it open rather than invent one.

The main gate is sometimes locked. There is a public entrance at the south end of the west fence, and daylight is the sensible time to go.
